verses.text: Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.
And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth;
Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

summary: This is the "more excellent way" Paul had just promised, and it opens not with a definition but with a series of demolitions in the first person. "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" — the most exalted speech imaginable reduced to temple noise. He escalates: "though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing," and then moves from endowment to sacrifice, "though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing." Three verdicts descend in order — worthless noise, then nothing, then no profit — so that the whole apparatus of gift, insight, generosity, and even martyrdom is set at zero without the one thing. Only then does Paul describe what charity is, and he does it almost entirely with verbs and mostly by negation: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things." Every clause reads like a line drawn against something the Corinthians had actually been doing. The argument then turns to duration, and here Paul makes his decisive point about the gifts they had been competing over: "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away." The reason is that all present spiritual knowledge is fragmentary — "we know in part, and we prophesy in part" — and fragments are made for a completion that will retire them: "when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away." Two images make this concrete without softening it. The first is growing up: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things." The second is a metal mirror's imperfect reflection: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known." The chapter ends with a triad and a ranking, and the ranking is the point: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."
takeaways: The chapter is an argument, not an ornament, and it is bolted to the chapters on either side of it. It answers the promise of chapter twelve, "yet shew I unto you a more excellent way," and is picked up immediately in the next line of chapter fourteen, "Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts." Charity is therefore not offered as an alternative to the gifts but as their measure and their governing habit, which is why Paul can command the pursuit of both in the same sentence. Read out of that setting the passage becomes a wedding poem; read in it, it is the answer to a church tearing itself apart over which endowments matter most.

The opening hypotheticals are all in the first person and all describe things Corinth admired. Angelic speech, prophecy, comprehension of "all mysteries, and all knowledge," mountain-moving faith, total almsgiving, and death by fire are the most impressive religious achievements available, and each is assigned a value of zero without charity. Notice the exact wording of the third verdict: "it profiteth me nothing." Paul had just said the Spirit's manifestations are given "to profit withal," meaning to profit others. A gift can genuinely benefit the church and still leave its bearer with nothing, which is a warning that usefulness and holiness are not the same measurement.

Charity is defined almost entirely by what it will not do. Of the fifteen clauses, most are refusals — "envieth not," "vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up," "Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil," "Rejoiceth not in iniquity." Each of these is a line drawn against something already documented in this letter: the envy behind the party slogans, the puffed-up boasting over teachers and knowledge, the unseemly behaviour at their meals, the self-seeking of those who insisted on their own rights. Paul does not describe charity as a feeling to be summoned but as a set of concrete behaviours to be practised, and he defines it in the vocabulary of their specific failures.

The four "all things" clauses — "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things" — are not a licence for credulity, because they stand immediately after "Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth." Charity's openness is bounded by truth: it refuses to take pleasure in wrongdoing even when doing so would be convenient, and it refuses to give up on a person even when doing so would be easier. The pairing keeps love from collapsing into either suspicion or sentimentality.

Paul's argument for the supremacy of charity is finally an argument about time. "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away." The gifts are provisional by design, and the reason given is not that they are defective but that they are partial: "we know in part, and we prophesy in part." To build an identity on a partial thing is to build on something scheduled for retirement. This applies as directly to theological knowledge as to tongues, and it should make anyone holding strong convictions hold them with the humility of a man looking "through a glass, darkly."

The closing triad ranks what abides. Faith, hope, and charity all continue where the charisms do not, but "the greatest of these is charity," and the reason lies in what happens at the consummation Paul has just described. When we see "face to face," faith turns into sight and hope turns into possession, while love has nothing to become because it is already the substance of the end. That makes charity not merely the best Christian behaviour in this life but the shape of eternal life itself, and it explains why a person with every gift and no love is, in Paul's blunt phrase, "nothing."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 12:31 — covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way
crossRefs.why: This chapter is the promised "more excellent way," and the specific gifts it relativizes are precisely the ones just listed — tongues, prophecy, knowledge, and mountain-moving faith all appear in the preceding catalogue. Reading the two together prevents the common mistake of treating chapter thirteen as a detachable meditation, since its whole force depends on the competitive scramble over charisms that chapter twelve describes.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 14:1 — Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy
crossRefs.why: The next verse resumes the argument without a pause and shows how charity is meant to be applied: it becomes the reason for preferring intelligible prophecy over an uninterpreted tongue, since love seeks the edification of the hearer rather than the satisfaction of the speaker. Chapter thirteen supplies the principle and chapter fourteen the rules that follow from it.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 22:37-40 — On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets
crossRefs.why: Paul's ranking of charity above every gift restates the ranking Jesus gave among the commandments, where love of God and neighbour is the hinge on which everything else turns. The parallel indicates that Paul is not introducing a novel Christian sentiment but applying the Lord's own ordering of the law to a dispute about spiritual endowments.

crossRefs.label: 1 John 4:8,20 — God is love... he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God
crossRefs.why: Where Paul argues that charity outlasts every gift, John supplies the reason by locating love in God's own nature, and he applies the same practical test Paul does: the claim to know God is falsified by failure to love the brother in view. The two passages together keep charity from being read as a merely human virtue or an emotional temperature rather than a participation in what God is.

crossRefs.label: Galatians 5:6,22 — faith which worketh by love... the fruit of the Spirit is love
crossRefs.why: The phrase "faith which worketh by love" bears directly on Paul's claim that "all faith, so that I could remove mountains" is nothing without charity, and it is the passage most often set beside this chapter in debates over how faith and love are related in justification. The listing of love as the first fruit of the Spirit also shows that charity is itself a work of the Spirit and not a human supplement to the Spirit's gifts.

crossRefs.label: Romans 13:10 — Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law
crossRefs.why: Paul's negative definitions here — charity "thinketh no evil" and "seeketh not her own" — are compressed in Romans into the principle that love "worketh no ill to his neighbour." The parallel confirms that the fifteen clauses are not poetic flourishes but a summary of what the commandments require, so that the behaviour described in this chapter is the law's actual content rather than an optional higher path.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading finds in this chapter the classic statement that faith is not saving unless it is informed by charity. Paul's own words are taken at full strength: "though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." A person may hold everything true and still be nothing, which is read as showing that charity is not an optional consequence appended to justifying faith but the very form that makes faith living. Faith, hope, and charity are understood as the three theological virtues poured into the soul, and the ranking "the greatest of these is charity" is heard as a statement of dignity and not merely of duration, since charity alone unites the soul directly to God and remains in glory when faith and hope have reached their term. On this reading the growth of the Christian life is measured by growth in charity, and the whole chapter serves as the standard by which any claim of grace, gift, or orthodoxy is finally tested.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters answer first from context: the subject under discussion is the spiritual endowments of chapter twelve, and "all faith, so that I could remove mountains" corresponds to the charism of faith listed there rather than to the trusting reliance on Christ by which a sinner is justified. Paul is not weighing love against saving faith; he is weighing love against the gifts Corinth was competing over. On the standard Protestant account, faith alone is the instrument that receives righteousness precisely because it is an empty hand rather than a virtue, yet faith is never alone in the person who has it, so a loveless faith is by definition a dead and counterfeit faith rather than a real faith lacking a supplement. Charity is called greatest because it endures without alteration into the world to come while faith passes into sight, not because it displaces faith as the means of union with Christ. Both traditions insist that a Christianity without love is worthless, that charity is the Spirit's work and not a human achievement, and that no orthodoxy or gift can substitute for it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "when that which is perfect is come" as the consummation, and "now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" as the scriptural anchor for the direct vision of God given to the blessed. The contrast is between knowing in part now and knowing hereafter "even as also I am known," which is a mutual and immediate knowledge that no book, no doctrine, and no accumulation of study can supply. On this reading the retirement of prophecy, tongues, and knowledge belongs to the end of all things and not to the close of the apostolic age, so nothing in this passage announces that the charisms would be withdrawn from the Church in history. The verse also grounds a deep reserve about theological certainty in this life, since even revealed knowledge is described as partial and mirror-like until the vision itself is given.

counterpoint.summary: Most Protestant interpreters agree that "that which is perfect" is the eschaton, on the plain ground that "face to face" and knowing "even as also I am known" describe the presence of God rather than any development within church history. A cessationist minority reads the perfect as the completed canon or the church's maturity, arguing that once revelation was fully given in writing the revelatory gifts had served their purpose and would "fail" and "cease" of themselves. Continuationists reply that the childhood analogy describes a change of state rather than the arrival of a document, and that no reader in any century has experienced the sight this passage promises. Both sides accept the passage's main claim, that present knowledge is genuinely partial, and both use it to argue for humility about what we think we have understood.
